fetched_contents.text: The Gendered Family Process Model: An Integrative Framework of Gender in the Family Abstract This article reviews and integrates research on gender-related biological, cognitive, and social processes that take place in or between family members, resulting in a newly developed gendered family process (GFP) model. The GFP model serves as a guiding framework for research on gender in the family context, calling for the integration of biological, social, and cognitive factors. Biological factors in the model are prenatal, postnatal, and pubertal androgen levels of children and parents, and genetic effects on parent and child gendered behavior. Social factors are family sex composition (i.e., parent sex, sexual orientation, marriage status, sibling sex composition) and parental gender socialization, such as modeling, gender-differentiated parenting, and gender talk. Cognitive factors are implicit and explicit gender-role cognitions of parents and children. Our review and the GFP model confirm that gender is an important organizer of family processes, but also highlight that much is still unclear about the mechanisms underlying gender-related processes within the family context. Therefore, we stress the need for (1) longitudinal studies that take into account the complex bidirectional relationship between parent and child gendered behavior and cognitions, in which within-family comparisons (comparing behavior of parents toward a boy and a girl in the same family) are made instead of between-family comparisons (comparing parenting between all-boy families and all-girl families, or between mixed-gender families and same-gender families), (2) experimental studies on the influence of testosterone on human gender development, (3) studies examining the interplay between biology with gender socialization and gender-role cognitions in humans. Keywords: Gender identity, Family process, Gender stereotypes, Gender socialization, Gender development Introduction Gender is one of the most important organizers of social life (Blakemore, Berenbaum, & Liben, 2009), from the cradle to the grave. It shapes a large part of children’s identity development, the way they view the world, and influences the way they are talked to, the way they are parented, the opportunities they are provided with, and people’s reactions to certain behaviors, hobbies, interests, and play styles. As a consequence of these processes, boys and girls differ, for example, in toy, occupational, and activity preferences throughout childhood and adolescence (e.g., Berenbaum, Martin, Hanish, Briggs, & Fabes, 2007; Konrad et al., 2000; McHale, Kim, Dotterer, Crouter, & Booth, 2009). Also, boys are more likely to express externalizing emotions and behaviors (e.g., aggression), whereas girls are more likely to show internalizing emotions and behaviors (e.g., depression) (for meta-analyses and reviews, see Archer, 2004; Chaplin & Aldao, 2013; Hyde, Mezulis, & Abrahamson, 2008). Children’s gender development can be studied in different contexts, such as the family context, the school context, the peer group, and the larger societal context (Blakemore et al., 2009). The current article reviews and integrates research on gender development of children and adolescents in the family context. The family context is crucial for gender development, providing the first gender-related experiences that children incorporate in their gender concepts (Bem, 1981), which in turn shape the influence of other socializing agents. Also, parents play a role in some of the biological factors (genes, prenatal testosterone) associated with child gender development (e.g., Caramaschi, Booij, Petitclerc, Boivin, & Tremblay, 2012). Several general and broad theories of child or gender development have been applied to gender socialization processes in the family context (e.g., evolutionary theories; Trivers, 1972; social role theory; Eagly, Wood, & Diekman, 2000; social learning theories; Bandura & Walters, 1963; Bussey & Bandura, 1999). However, these theories do not specifically address gender-related family processes, i.e., all gender-related biological, cognitive, and social processes that take place in or between members of the family (Whitechurch & Constantine, 1993). For example, evolutionary theories predict that different behaviors are adaptive for males and females, but are applied primarily to gender differences in aggression and parental investment. Social role theory attributes differences in behavior of women and men to the contrasting distributions of men and women into social roles, and primarily tries to explain (bio)social gendered processes not limited to the family context (Wood & Eagly, 2012). Social learning theory predicts the development of social behaviors from processes such as observational learning and reinforcement/punishment from social agents in the child’s environment. There are also some family context frameworks or models that mainly focus on very specific gender-related aspects or processes in the family system, such as children’s gender cognitions (e.g., gender-schema theories; Bem, 1981, 1983; Martin & Halverson, 1981, 1987), or integrate biological and environmental factors in a family system, but are not focused on gender (e.g., genotype–environment effects; Scarr & McCartney, 1983). Previous reviews provided valuable overviews of biological, social, or cognitive perspectives on children’s gender development in the family context, but did not integrate these different perspectives (see Blakemore et al., 2009; Eccles, Freedman-Doan, Frome, Jacobs, & Yoon, 2000; Maccoby & Jacklin, 1974; McHale, Crouter, & Whiteman, 2003). Several gender development scholars have signaled the need for a comprehensive explanatory model combining biological, social, and cognitive perspectives on gender development (e.g., Berenbaum, Martin, & Ruble, 2008; Berenbaum, Blakemore, & Beltz, 2011; Leaper, 2015). fetched_contents.text: Gender Development - an overview Chapters and Articles You might find these chapters and articles relevant to this topic. Abstract Gender development takes on new meaning in adolescence as girls and boys experience physical, cognitive, and social changes to prepare them for their adult roles as women and men. This article reviews prominent explanations of adolescent gender-role development, including the effects of sex hormones and the brain, and evolutionary, cognitive, gender schema, social-cognitive, social structural, and gender intensification theories of development. The article also considers how families, peers, schools, the larger community, and the mass media socialize adolescents into gender roles. Finally, the authors examine empirical evidence regarding adolescent gender development across the domains of gender-role identity, gender role attitudes, gendered behavior, and mental health. Read full chapter URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780123739513000570 1 Overview of Gender Development In recent years, gender has come to be viewed as a multidimensional construct that covers many domains including biological sex, activities and interests, personal–social attributes, gender-based social relationships, gender-based styles and symbols (such as gestures, style of dress), and gender-related values (see Ruble and Martin 1998, Huston 1983). Each domain can be examined in terms of an individual's concepts, self-perceptions, preferences, and behaviors. In the past, there was an implicit assumption that a person who was gender typed in one domain also was gender typed in other domains. The multidimensional view of gender has been useful in questioning this assumption and replacing it with the challenge to researchers that interrelations among domains need to be assessed. Also, this view has the advantage of making clear the distinctions among the different domains. Certain aspects of gender development have been investigated more than others, including gender roles, self-perceptions of gender, gender identity, and gender-related behaviors. Gender roles have been a popular topic of study, within both psychology and sociology. Gender role is a broad term referring to the behaviors, attitudes, and traits that are associated with being male or female. Many studies have been done to identify the roles that men and women fulfill in western cultures as well as in other countries and in our history. Gender stereotypes, which are culturally defined expectations about the sexes in terms of personality, appearance, occupations, abilities, and interests, have been a very central subject for social psychologists. Also, psychologists have been involved in studying self-perceptions of gender, especially individual's perceptions of masculinity and femininity. Gender identity, the sense of oneself as being a male or female, has been studied by clinical and developmental psychologists, whereas a typical gender identity has been investigated largely by medical researchers. Gender-related behaviors and characteristics have been the subject of numerous studies, including how children develop skills and social behaviors such as their relationship preferences. Read full chapter URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B0080430767016843 4 Gender development and socialization of aggression A large body of research suggests that children are attuned to cues about gender as early as infancy and develop an increasingly complex understanding of gender and gender identity across development (Levy & Haaf, 1994; Quinn et al., 2002). Children first acquire gender stereotypes relating to what activities and behaviors, including aggression, are appropriate for boys and girls early in childhood (Martin and Ruble, 2010). Gender schema theory and social-cognitive theory of gender development are complementary theories that can be used to understand how gender identity and gendered behaviors, including components of the SIP model and aggressive behaviors, develop. 4.1 Theories of gender development Gender schemas are cognitive structures that children develop to organize gender-related information about what it means to be a woman or man in one's culture (Bem, 1981; Martin & Halverson, 1981). According to gender schema theory, children construct a simple “in-group/out-group schema” to classify the extent to which certain objects, behaviors, and roles are for boys or girls (Martin & Halverson, 1981). Information that is consistent with a child's gender schemas is more likely to be encoded and remembered while information inconsistent with these schemas is ignored. Further, when a child integrates gender-related information into their “own-sex schema,” they are then motivated to behave in ways compatible with their own-sex schema for activities (e.g., boys play with trucks, girls play with dolls), roles (e.g., men are police officers), and traits (e.g., women are nice), also known as gender-linked conduct (Martin and Ruble, 2010). ## Mini-report on Block’s model and its integration of biology, culture, and cognition

Block’s model, as summarized in the provided evidence, is best understood as an **integrative framework** that combines **biological, cognitive, and social factors** into one developmental account of gender-related processes, especially within the family context [N1-F1]. The core components are organized around three broad domains: **biological**, **social**, and **cognitive** factors, with the family serving as a central setting where these processes interact [N1-F1]. In other words, the model does not treat these domains as separate explanations; it treats them as mutually connected influences on how gendered behavior, cognitions, and social practices develop [N1-F1].

### Core components and organization
The model is described as a “gendered family process model,” which means it focuses on **family processes** rather than gender in isolation [N1-F1]. Within this framework, the biological component includes **prenatal, postnatal, and pubertal androgen levels** of children and parents, as well as **genetic effects** on parent and child gendered behavior [N2-R1]. The social component includes **family sex composition** (parent sex, sexual orientation, marriage status, sibling sex composition) and **parental gender socialization**, such as **modeling, gender-differentiated parenting, and gender talk** [N3-R1]. The cognitive component includes **implicit and explicit gender-role cognitions** of parents and children [N1-F1].

So the model is organized around a tripartite structure:
- **Biological**: hormone levels and genes
- **Social**: family structure and socialization practices
- **Cognitive**: gender-related beliefs and schemas [N1-F1][N3-R1][N2-R1]

### Biology as a predisposition or constraint
In Block’s model, biology is not treated as a fixed destiny but as a **predisposition or constraint** that influences, but does not determine, gendered development [N2-R2]. The evidence states that biological predispositions may influence gender behavior, while socialization plays a significant role in how individuals express those behaviors [N2-R2]. It also notes that biological sex is a complex, multidimensional construct influenced by anatomy, genetics, and hormones, and that oversimplifying it ignores scientific reality [N2-R3]. In the family process model, biological factors include prenatal, postnatal, and pubertal androgen levels and genetic effects, which suggests biology operates across development rather than only at birth [N2-R1].

### Culture as a social context and practice
Culture is operationalized in Block’s model as the **social context and practice** through which gender-related information is transmitted across generations [N3-R4][N3-R5]. The model explicitly includes **family sex composition** and **parental gender socialization** as social factors [N3-R1]. The evidence also notes that gender socialization is defined as the process by which cultural information about gender is transmitted across generations, shaping behaviors, values, and expectations [N3-R4]. In addition, the family context is described as the first gender-related experiences children incorporate into their gender concepts, and it shapes the influence of other socializing agents [N1-F1]. This means culture in Block’s model is not abstract; it is embedded in **family structure, parenting practices, and the broader social environment** that children experience.

### Cognition as mediator of interpretation and behavior
Cognition in the model mediates how children **interpret** and **act out** gendered information. The evidence states that **gender schemas** are cognitive structures that children develop to organize gender-related information about what it means to be a woman or man in one’s culture [N4-R3][N4-F2]. Gender schema theory explains that children encode and remember information consistent with their schemas while ignoring inconsistent information, and that they are motivated to behave in ways compatible with their own-sex schema for activities, roles, and traits [N4-F2]. Social-cognitive theory extends this by describing how **motivational, self-regulatory, and environmental factors** interact to shape gender development [N4-F2]. So cognition does not merely reflect culture; it actively organizes cultural inputs into interpretations and behaviors.

The model’s strength is its **integration**: biology sets the starting point and constraints, culture provides the social context and practices, and cognition translates those inputs into interpretation and action [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-R1][N4-F2]. The evidence explicitly calls for an integrated framework that combines biological, social, and cognitive factors [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that gender is an important organizer of family processes, but much remains unclear about the mechanisms underlying those processes [N1-F1]. That said, the provided evidence supports the model as a coherent attempt to move beyond single-factor explanations and toward a more developmental, bidirectional account of gendered behavior [N1-F1].

The evidence compares Block’s model with several alternative perspectives. ## Mini-report on Block’s model and its integration of biology, culture, and cognition

The model is described as a “gendered family process model,” which means it focuses on **family processes** rather than gender in isolation [N1-F1]. Within this framework, the biological component includes **prenatal, postnatal, and pubertal androgen levels** of children and parents, as well as **genetic effects** on parent and child gendered behavior [N2-R1]. The social component includes **family sex composition** (parent sex, sexual orientation, marriage status, sibling sex composition) and **parental gender socialization**, such as **modeling, gender-differentiated parenting, and gender talk** [N3-R1]. The cognitive component includes **implicit and explicit gender-role cognitions** of parents and children [N1-F1].

So the model is organized around a tripartite structure:
- **Biological**: hormone levels and genes
- **Social**: family structure and socialization practices
- **Cognitive**: gender-related beliefs and schemas [N1-F1][N3-R1][N2-R1]

### Biology as a predisposition or constraint
In Block’s model, biology is not treated as a fixed destiny but as a **predisposition or constraint** that influences, but does not determine, gendered development [N2-R2]. The evidence states that biological predispositions may influence gender behavior, while socialization plays a significant role in how individuals express those behaviors [N2-R2]. So cognition does not merely reflect culture; it actively organizes cultural inputs into interpretations and behaviors.

### Overall integration
The model’s strength is its **integration**: biology sets the starting point and constraints, culture provides the social context and practices, and cognition translates those inputs into interpretation and action [N1-F1][N2-R1][N3-R1][N4-F2]. The evidence explicitly calls for an integrated framework that combines biological, social, and cognitive factors [N1-F1].
